title: Conclusion — Acting Apart
paragraphs: Sen does not die. He spends a year bedridden; then a masseuse friend works his wasted legs, and he crawls to a lamp, stands, walks, cooks, rides a bicycle. The doctor calls it a miracle. The family calls it karma. Sen calls it neither: "The real reason I got better is that I did it myself: I let go."

That sentence is the book's final reversal. Letting go — which a Western reader has spent seven sections wanting to call passivity — returns as the very shape of agency, spoken by the man everyone had let go of. Karma, Sen adds with a grin, is what bound his story to Julia's: they must have met before, in some other life.

The town rearranges itself around the recovery. Gaew closes the shop and opens a noodle stand; the family aunt runs the new 7-Eleven, alcohol-free; Aung keeps Julia posted across the ocean; Goy — still reading, still cool — closes the frame her father's death opened.

The Conclusion then widens into argument. Mae Jaeng's model of agency-through-acceptance is locally hegemonic and globally counter-hegemonic: it sits at odds with the biomedicine of its own hospitals, whose Buddhist doctors nonetheless treat "not Buddhistly." The author argues for medicine that works with local religious healing rather than against it, and for a psychology honest about the particular (Western, urban, rich) places its "universals" were made.

The Buddhism described here, Cassaniti insists, is not Buddhism-in-general: it is particular to a Northern Thai valley at a particular time — and that particularity is the point. Understanding it widens the toolkit of anyone, anywhere, who has to live in a world that will not stop changing.

The last move is the title's: read "living" not as an adjective but as a verb. An objective fact is always also a subjective one, and Buddhism in practice — living Buddhism — is how one Thai community makes that true, day by cool-hearted day.
